newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe dollar seen steady in coming months.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe dollar seen steady in coming months.

text.p: The Zimbabwe dollar is likely to trade largely unchanged against major currencies in coming months despite an anticipated large inflow of foreign currency from annual tobacco sales, market analysts said on Wednesday.

Tobacco officials expect 214 million kg of the crop to go under the hammer in the marketing season running to October, earning the country over Z$8 billion (U.S.$708 million) in foreign exchange, up from Z$6.8 billion (U.S.$601.8 million) last year.

Local foreign exchange dealers told Reuters they expected the Zimbabwe dollar -- which fell by over 15 percent against the U.S. dollar last year -- to drift downwards to 11.40 against the key U.S. dollar by October from about 11.30 at present.
They said the central Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe would probably seek to protect exporters by constantly intervening to mop up any excess funds in the market and keep a tight grip on exchange rates.

"If I were to take into consideration what the Reserve Bank has been doing lately I think the rates won't move much. Their aim seems to be to encourage exports by maintaining a weak Zimbabwe dollar," one dealer said. "There is also still some element of importer demand which will probably cancel out the effect of tobacco inflows."
Edmore Tobaiwa, chief economist at the Zimbabwe National Chamber of Commerce (ZNCC), said the Zimbabwe dollar could actually lose between 0.1 and 0.2 percentage points in the next month.
He said President Robert Mugabe's government was absorbing most of the export earnings to fund its huge spending, estimated at around 38 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
"The growth of credit to the government (from domestic borrowing) is pegged at more than 35 percent and it's crowding out the private sector," he said, adding it should ideally be around 25 percent.

Private economic consultant John Robertson feels it would be in the interests of the southern Africa country's economy to maintain a weak currency, saying the Zimbabwe dollar is overvalued at the moment.
"It's particularly difficult for our exports. For instance, the tobacco people and the gold miners won't be happy with an appreciation of the currency," Robertson said.

Since the tobacco floors opened some two weeks ago, only a few pockets of foreign currency earnings have found their way into the market. Dealers say growers could be holding back their earnings to allow for a slight Zimbabwe dollar depreciation to afford them better profits.
"It seems likely that the Reserve Bank will have to intervene. I believe the exporters are the people that we have to look after," Robertson told Reuters. ($=Z$11.30)
